units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Turn one step of a linear recurrence into a companion matrix, so n steps are the n-th power, and take that power by squaring once per bit of n and multiplying in at the one bits: floor(log2 n) + popcount(n) - 1 products instead of n - 1, for Fibonacci at a quintillion, for walk counts on a graph, for anything associative.
units.description: Matrix exponentiation by squaring: F(20,000), 4,180 digits, from 18 matrix products equal to 20,000 iteration steps with Cassini's identity holding; F(10^18) mod 10^9 + 7 agreed by the matrix, fast doubling, and Kitamasa (209783453) in 656, 180, and 492 scalar multiplications; the product count exactly floor(log2 n) + popcount(n) - 1 on every n to 4,096; A^L equal to a walk count; recursion 1,664,079 calls for F(30).

units.plan_row: Matrix exponentiation × Binary exponentiation. Puzzle 185, optimization-or (problemSlug linear-recurrences, the atlas problem page carrying "Linear recurrence evaluation"; sibling live lesson modular-exponentiation-square-multiply, puzzle 128). Solution matrix_exponentiation_binary_exponentiation.py (0.2s, prints OK): a counting matrix multiply, binary exponentiation for matrices and integers, iterative and recursive Fibonacci, fast doubling, Kitamasa's polynomial method, companion matrices, an iterative recurrence evaluator, and a walk-counting dynamic program. ORACLES: (1) exact: F(n) by matrix equals iteration for n = 1, 2, 10, 93, 1,000, 20,000 (4,180 digits; 18 matrix products against 20,000 steps), Cassini F(n-1)F(n+1) - F(n)^2 = (-1)^n at 20,000; (2) n = 10^18 mod 10^9+7: matrix, fast doubling, Kitamasa all 209783453, scalar multiplications 656 (59 squarings + 23 multiplies = 82 products) / 180 / 492; a random order-5 recurrence at n = 100,000: iteration 99,996 steps (499,980 multiplications), companion 23 products (2,875), Kitamasa 22 products (850), all equal, and equal for n = 0 to 39; at 10^18 companion 12,125 against Kitamasa 3,595; (3) products = floor(log2 n) + popcount(n) - 1 for every n to 4,096 and 50 random 64-bit n (mean 92.9 against n - 1 ~ 10^19); 1,000 modular powers equal pow(); (4) A^L equal to the walk DP for L = 1 to 12 on a 7-vertex graph (A^12 in 4 products); (5) recursive F(30) 1,664,079 calls = 2F(31) - 1 in 0.09 s; iteration 0.045 s per million steps so 10^18 is about 1,400 years; the matrix power at 10^18 in 0.09 ms. Honest: fast doubling (180) and Kitamasa (492, 3,595) beat the matrix's constants; author correction recorded (the draft claimed the matrix was cheaper than doubling). Cards: self, Kitamasa's algorithm, Fibonacci DP, Modular exponentiation (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: iteration or naive recursion when n has eighteen digits. Figure: the 60 bits of 10^18 with the induced squarings and multiplies beside a log-scale bar chart of scalar multiplications by method; cite Knuth TAOCP 2 4.6.3 and 1 1.2.8, Pingala, al-Kashi. Viz MatrixPowerViz: binary exponentiation of the Fibonacci matrix mod 10^9+7 for a seeded 30-to-50-bit exponent, one bit per tick, result and base matrices drawn, the product counter against n - 1, the partial result checked against fast doubling on every tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 450, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Rent for 1 a day or buy for B with the season length unknown: rent until the rent paid would equal the price, then buy on day B. Whatever day the season ends you pay at most 2 − 1/B times the clairvoyant, and no deterministic rule does better; a coin gets e/(e − 1), a trusted forecast gets more and risks everything.
units.description: Break-even ski rental by exact enumeration: threshold k = B has worst-case ratio exactly 2 − 1/B at every price 2 to 100, every other threshold strictly worse (neighbours 2, day one B, 2B gives 3 − 1/B); the randomized KMMO rule reaches 1.5353 at B = 10, equalized over every season length; a trusted distribution beats both, 10.00 against 13.70.
units.time: O(1) per day: one counter against B
units.baseline: Buy on day one / never buy

units.plan_row: Ski rental × Break-even deterministic rule. Puzzle 186, optimization-or (problemSlug optimal-stopping, the atlas problem page carrying "Rent-or-buy decisions"; sibling live lesson secretary-one-over-e, puzzle 108). Solution ski_rental_break_even_deterministic_rule.py (0.5s, prints OK): a cost function for any buy-day threshold, the clairvoyant min(T, B), a worst-case scorer over every season length, the Karlin-Manasse-McGeoch-Owicki distribution and its expected ratio, an expected-cost evaluator for a known season distribution, and a geometric season generator, all in exact Fractions. ORACLES: (1) for B in {2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100}, every threshold k in 1..3B against every T in 1..3B: k = B is the unique best with ratio exactly 2 - 1/B (1.5, 1.6667, 1.8, 1.9, 1.95, 1.98, 1.99); k < B scores 1 + (B - 1)/k, k > B scores (k - 1 + B)/B, both neighbours exactly 2, k = 1 scores B, k = 2B scores 3 - 1/B (2.9 at B = 10); (2) the randomized rule's worst expected ratio equals 1/(1 - (1 - 1/B)^B) exactly: 1.3333, 1.4874, 1.5353, 1.5774 at B = 2, 5, 10, 100 against the limit e/(e - 1) = 1.5820 (within 0.006 at B = 100), every season length equalized (all ratios equal), 20,000-trial Monte Carlo at B = 10 within four standard errors (worst sampled 1.538 +/- 0.015); (3) stochastic seasons at B = 10: geometric mean 5: Bayes never buys 5.000, break-even 5.671, randomized 6.852, buy day one 10, clairvoyant 4.463; geometric mean 20: Bayes buys day 1 for 10.000, break-even 13.698, randomized 12.322, never buy 19.999, clairvoyant 8.025; half 3-day half 40-day: Bayes day 4 for 8.000, break-even 11.000, randomized 9.980, clairvoyant 6.500; (4) negative examples at B = 10: buy on day one ratio 10 on a one-day season, never buy ratio 3 at 30 days and unbounded, threshold 2B ratio 2.90. Honest: a coin beats the hero (1.5353 against 1.9), a trusted distribution beats both, break-even beats the randomized rule at mean 5 and loses at mean 20. Two author corrections recorded: the draft claimed randomized beats break-even on every distribution (mean 5 refutes it), and wrote the 2B ratio as 4 - 1/B and the early thresholds as a flat 2 (enumeration: 3 - 1/B and 1 + (B - 1)/k). Cards: self (algoName Ski rental), Ski rental x Randomized exponential threshold (algoName Ski rental), Secretary problem x 1/e stopping rule (algoName Secretary problem, puzzle 108 named in when), Multiplicative weights update (algoName); all four pages verified in dist/algo. neverUse: tuning the threshold to a forecast when the future is adversarial (buy day one ratio B, never buy unbounded, both Bayes-optimal for some distribution). Figure: worst-case ratio against buy-day threshold at B = 10 with the unique minimum at k = B, beside cost against season length for the clairvoyant, break-even, randomized expectation, buy day one, and never buy; cite Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph, Sleator, Algorithmica 1988, DOI 10.1007/BF01762111, and Karlin, Manasse, McGeoch, Owicki, Algorithmica 1994. Viz SkiRentalViz: one season per cycle, one day per tick, seeded price 6..12 and hidden season length, four rules paying day by day (break-even, randomized with a seeded KMMO draw, buy day one, never buy) against the clairvoyant line and the (2 - 1/B) bound; invariants every day: break-even cost <= (2 - 1/B) x min(d, B) and the randomized expectation = ratio x min(d, B) (equalizing); NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 12.35 ticks per cycle, max 32, 0 breaks; stepMs 450, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Give every block a gen set (its last write of each variable) and a kill set (every other definition of those variables), start all IN and OUT empty, and pop blocks off a worklist seeded in reverse postorder: IN is the union of the predecessors' OUT, OUT is gen plus whatever in IN survives kill, and a successor is re-queued only when OUT changed; because union distributes over these transfer functions, the fixpoint is exactly the meet over all paths, reached in about two visits per block.
units.description: Reaching definitions by a worklist in reverse postorder on 300 structured programs: equal to a per-definition search and to 8,462,078 enumerated walks on all 300; 24,767 visits over 12,815 blocks against 46,833 round robin and 171,343 against the flow; all 18,405 executed use-def pairs allowed; one sweep without iteration missed 26,421 facts.
units.time: O(blocks × depth) visits, a set union per edge
units.space: two sets per block (IN and OUT)
units.plan_row: Reaching definitions × Forward dataflow. Puzzle 187, languages-compilers (problemSlug dataflow-analysis, the atlas problem page carrying "Dataflow analysis"; no live sibling on this problem; nearest live lesson register-allocation-graph-coloring, puzzle 162, whose liveness input is this analysis run backward). Solution reaching_definitions_forward_dataflow.py (4.9s, prints OK): a three-address IR over four variables, a random structured-program generator (sequences, if/else, while, nested to depth 3; 300 programs, 12,815 blocks, 42.7 on average and 206 at most, 23,841 definitions, 28,245 uses, 224 programs with a loop, loop-depth histogram 76 / 63 / 121 / 40 for depths 0 to 3), gen/kill per block, reverse postorder by DFS, a worklist solver (seeded in a given order, successors re-queued on OUT change; optionally drawing the next block at random), a round-robin solver asserting monotonicity on every visit, a single-sweep solver, a per-definition reachability referee, an exhaustive bounded-walk referee (every walk from the entry visiting no block more than twice), use-def chains, and a concrete-execution simulator (120 runs per program, branches by parity, loop cap 6 visits, step cap 600). ORACLES: (1) worklist fixpoint equal to the per-definition referee AND to the bounded-walk union on all 300 programs (8,462,078 walks enumerated, 3,444,766 on the largest program; 87,308 reaching facts in total); (2) no IN or OUT set ever shrank between round-robin passes; round robin in reverse postorder within depth + 2 passes on every program (982 passes total, max 5, the bound tight on 257 of 300); the four iterating solvers return identical sets; visits strictly ordered: worklist rpo 24,767 visits / 79,058 set ops, worklist random order 38,379 / 123,078 (worst program 2.8x the rpo visits; no worse than rpo on 20 of 300), round robin rpo 46,833 / 147,363, round robin against the flow (reversed rpo) 171,343 / 539,561 in 3,105 passes (max 22); per block 1.93 / 2.99 / 3.65 / 13.4; (3) all 18,405 executed use-def pairs inside the 40,971 chains the analysis allows (44.9% exercised); 8,200 dead stores flagged, none read in any execution; 7,453 definitions never read in 120 runs that the analysis could not rule out (the measured imprecision); (4) the single forward sweep: 26,421 reaching facts missing, wrong on all 224 looping programs (exact only on the 76 loop-free ones), use-def chains unsound on 163 programs (4,005 executed pairs denied). Honest: the random worklist order is no worse on 20 shallow programs; the analysis is path-insensitive (44.9% of chains exercised, 7,453 never-read definitions not ruled out); one author correction recorded (the draft's exhaustive referee enumerated simple paths only and failed on the first loop, since a body definition reaches the loop exit only through a path visiting the head twice; two visits per block is exactly enough). Cards: self (Reaching definitions), Live variable analysis, Available expressions, Constant propagation (all algoName, pages present in dist/algo). neverUse: a single forward sweep that never revisits a block. Figure: a five-block loop with IN sets after pass 1 and pass 2 (the single sweep folds c = a to 1, wrong) beside block visits per block by schedule; cite Kildall POPL 1973 DOI 10.1145/512927.512945, Hecht and Ullman SIAM J. Computing 1975, Kam and Ullman Acta Informatica 1977, Aho/Lam/Sethi/Ullman ch. 9. Viz ReachingDefinitionsViz: a seeded structured program of 7 to 14 blocks drawn in reverse postorder (forward edges below, back edges above in amber), the worklist solver one block visit per tick with each block filling by the share of its final reaching set learned, the queue as a strip, invariant every tick that every IN/OUT set is below the per-definition oracle and never shrinks, equality with the oracle at the end and the single sweep's deficit reported; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles (20.8 ticks per cycle, up to 45), 0 breaks; stepMs 420, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Take any tour, find two edges whose swap (reconnect a to c and b to d, reversing the path between them) is shorter, apply it, and repeat until a full pass finds none: in the plane every crossing is such a swap, so the local optimum is crossing-free, each test costs four distance lookups, and sorted neighbor lists make a pass near-linear.
units.description: 2-opt tour improvement against an exact Held-Karp referee on twenty 16-city instances: 1.85% above optimal from nearest neighbor (optimal 13 of 20), 0.00% with Or-opt; zero crossings at every local optimum from 16 to 1,600 cities; 400 cities untangled in 103 swaps and 46 ms; neighbor lists of twenty cut 40.9M lookups to 2.95M.
units.time: O(n²) per pass, O(nk) with neighbor lists, passes until one is clean
units.space: the tour and a position array
units.plan_row: 2-opt × Edge-uncrossing swaps. Puzzle 188, optimization-or (problemSlug traveling-salesman, the atlas problem page carrying "Tour improvement"; sibling live lessons annealing-cooling 2, held-karp-bitmask-states 81, christofides-matching-euler-tour 117). Solution two_opt_edge_uncrossing_swaps.py (13.3 s, prints OK): distance matrix, nearest neighbor, segment-intersection crossing counter, sorted neighbor lists, 2-opt (first- or best-improvement, full scan or Johnson-McGeoch neighbor-list candidates in both tour directions, shorter-side reversal), Or-opt (runs of 1 to 3, both orientations), Held-Karp bitmask DP, brute force. ORACLES: (1) Held-Karp equals brute force at n = 9; twenty random instances at n = 16, exact gap over the optimum: nearest neighbor mean 14.98% max 41.60% optimal 1/20; 2-opt from NN mean 1.85% max 8.31% optimal 13/20; 2-opt then Or-opt 0.00% optimal 20/20; 2-opt from random mean 4.12% max 17.93% optimal 8/20; crossings over the 20 instances NN 30, random 491, every 2-opt local optimum 0; Held-Karp total 3.5 s; (2) zero crossings at every full-neighborhood local optimum at n = 100, 200, 400, 800, 1,600 (NN starts had 17 / 24 / 32 / 62 / 147 crossings, random starts 1,026 / 5,068 / 18,278 / 69,376), every accepted delta negative and the deltas summing to the length change, every tour a permutation; (3) n = 400 (BHH estimate 14.25): NN 18.472 (1.296x), 79,800 lookups, 32 crossings; 2-opt full scan 16.241 (1.140x) 1,369,560 lookups 103 moves 46 ms 0 crossings; neighbor lists k=10 15.802, 185,618 lookups, 110 moves, 17 ms, 0 crossings; k=20 15.802, 186,230, 110 moves, 18 ms, 0; 2-opt then Or-opt 15.664 (1.099x) +3,824,750 lookups +41 moves 138 ms; random tour 203.411 (14.276x) 18,278 crossings; 2-opt from random 16.766 (1.177x) 2,223,069 lookups 2,334 moves 78 ms; n = 1,600: NN 36.930 (147 crossings); full scan 31.579 (1.108x) 40,919,705 lookups 523 moves 1,927 ms 0 crossings; k=10 31.254, 3,086,785 lookups, 5 crossings; k=20 31.010, 2,951,243 lookups, 304 ms, 0 crossings; n = 800: full 22.225 / k=20 22.038 / Or-opt 21.623 / from random 23.156 in 5,700 moves; (4) first vs best improvement, n = 100, ten instances, means: NN first 8.291 (79,192 lookups, 36 moves), NN best 8.171 (298,860, 19), random first 8.561 (112,941, 401), random best 8.362 (1,519,205, 103). Honest: AUTHOR CORRECTIONS recorded in the file: the draft expected neighbor lists of ten to lose nothing (they left 5 crossings at n = 1,600; twenty was clean at every size for a seventh to a fourteenth of the lookups), expected first and best improvement to tie (best is 1.4% / 2.3% shorter at 3.8x / 13.5x the lookups), and the neighbor-list scan landed on a shorter local optimum than the full scan at every size (a different path, not a bigger neighborhood). Cards: self (2-opt), Or-opt, Lin-Kernighan, Simulated annealing (live lesson badge, puzzle 2) (all algoName, all pages in dist/algo). neverUse: Held-Karp or any exact search at n = 400 (0.18 s per 16-city instance, doubling per city, 2^400 states). Figure: the uncrossing geometry (red removed pair, amber added pair, the triangle inequality at the crossing point X) beside a bar chart of the exact gaps at n = 16 with optimal counts; cite Croes 1958 Operations Research DOI 10.1287/opre.6.6.791, Flood 1956, Johnson and McGeoch 1997. units.oneLiner: Seal the bids, give the item to the highest, and charge the second bid: your bid then decides only whether you win, never what you pay, so the truth is a dominant strategy, the highest value always wins, and the seller earns exactly what a first-price auction would at equilibrium, without anyone computing one.
units.description: The Vickrey auction against exhaustive deviation checks and closed forms: 0 profitable deviations in 4,029,261 comparisons; the highest value wins 60,000 of 60,000 draws; revenue 0.4997 at n = 3 against first-price 0.4994 and theory 0.5; Myerson's reserve 0.5 lifts two-bidder revenue from 0.333 to 0.418; a seller shill steals 0.2496 per sale.
units.time: O(n log n) to sort the bids, O(n) with two running maxima
units.plan_row: Vickrey auction × Second-price rule. Puzzle 189, optimization-or (problemSlug auction-design, the atlas problem page carrying "Truthful single-item auction"; sibling live lessons gale-shapley-deferred-acceptance, puzzle 73, and secretary-one-over-e). Solution vickrey_auction_second_price_rule.py (0.76s, prints OK): a Vickrey auction with optional reserve, a first-price auction, an ascending clock auction, second-price and first-price payoff functions, the expected first-price payoff against equilibrium rivals, the closed-form two-bidder reserve revenue 1/3 + r^2 - 4r^3/3, and a mean with standard error. ORACLES, i.i.d. uniform [0, 1] values, 60,000 draws per cell: (1) dominant strategy exhaustively: 21 values x 21 highest rival bids x 21 deviations = 9,261 grid comparisons plus 20,000 random continuous profiles x 201 deviations = 4,020,000, total 4,029,261 comparisons, 0 profitable deviations from the truth; under a first-price rule 210 of the 441 grid (value, rival) cells reward shading; (2) first-price equilibrium by best response: against rivals bidding (n - 1)v/n, the best reply on a 1,000-bid grid is within 0.0007 of (n - 1)v/n over n = 2, 3, 5 and v = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, and bidding v earns exactly 0 (equilibrium utility 0.149 on average); (3) revenue equivalence: Vickrey 0.3351 +/- 0.0010, 0.4997 +/- 0.0009, 0.6665 +/- 0.0007 at n = 2, 3, 5 against first-price at equilibrium 0.3340 +/- 0.0005, 0.4994 +/- 0.0005, 0.6668 +/- 0.0005 and theory (n - 1)/(n + 1) = 0.3333, 0.5, 0.6667, all within three standard errors; the highest value won 60,000 of 60,000 at every n; an ascending clock at increment 0.001 matched the Vickrey winner on 3,000 of 3,000 draws and the price within 0.001, 500 rounds per auction on average; (4) Myerson's reserve: the closed form peaks at r = 0.500 on a 1,000-point grid; simulated two-bidder revenue 0.3330 +/- 0.0010 (r = 0, formula 0.3333), 0.3859 +/- 0.0008 (0.3, formula 0.3873), 0.4181 +/- 0.0010 (0.5, formula 0.4167), 0.3674 +/- 0.0015 (0.7, formula 0.3660), each within three standard errors, 0.5 the best; unsold 0%, 9.2%, 24.7%, 48.8%; (5) efficiency and the negative example: Vickrey misallocates on 0 of 60,000 draws; a first-price auction between a bidder shading by half and one shading by a fifth misallocates 18.7% of draws and loses 3.5% of welfare; a seller who reads the bids and shills just under the winner extracts 0.2496 +/- 0.0008 per sale at n = 3, the whole gap E[v1 - v2] = 1/(n + 1) = 0.25. Author correction recorded (the draft called the two-bidder reserve gain a third; the formula gives 1/3 to 5/12, a quarter). Cards: self, VCG mechanism, Myerson optimal auction, Ascending clock auction (all algoName; pages verified in dist/algo). neverUse: the second-price rule with a seller who can read the bids (the shill) or colluding bidders. Figure: payoff against bid for a bidder with value 0.8 facing a rival bid of 0.5 under both rules (the second-price step, flat above the rival, truth optimal; first-price 0.8 - b, truth earns 0) beside the two-bidder revenue curve against the reserve with four measured points peaking at 0.5; cite Vickrey 1961 Journal of Finance DOI 10.1111/j.1540-6261.1961.tb02789.x, Myerson 1981, Clarke 1971, Groves 1973. Viz VickreyViz: sixty three-bidder sealed-bid auctions, one per tick, bars for the bids with the winner green and the amber second-price line, a probed bidder's payoff-against-bid step curve, running Vickrey and equilibrium first-price revenue against (n - 1)/(n + 1) = 0.5; invariant every tick: the highest value wins, pays the second value, and 41 probed deviations never beat the truth; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 60 ticks, 0 breaks (2,460 deviations per cycle); stepMs 420, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Scan the pixels once in reading order, giving each foreground pixel the label of a neighbor already seen or a fresh one, record every meeting of two labels as a union, then rewrite each label to its root in a second pass: two streaming reads, no stack, no recursion, and a merge-only table sized by labels, not pixels.
units.description: Two-pass labeling against a flood-fill referee: equal partitions on 88 image-connectivity pairs; 38,400 visits (two per pixel) against 41,280 and 63,360; 179 and 78 provisional labels for 28 and 27 blobs merged by 151 and 51 unions at 0.635 and 0.405 links per find; a 3,220-pixel snake crashes a recursive fill; the naive single pass splits every U.
units.time: O(n α(n)): two passes over n pixels, near-constant per union and find
units.space: O(L) parent and rank entries for L provisional labels, plus the label image
units.baseline: Breadth-first flood fill from every unlabeled pixel
units.plan_row: Connected component labeling × Two-pass union-find. Puzzle 190, signal-graphics (problemSlug region-labeling, the atlas problem page carrying "Region labeling"; sibling live lessons canny-edge-detector-hysteresis-thresholding, puzzle 173, and unionfind-rank-compression, puzzle 8). Solution connected_component_labeling_two_pass_union_find.py (0.3s, prints OK): a counting union-find (unions, finds, parent links followed) with path compression and union by rank, the two-pass labeler (visits, provisional labels), an iterative BFS flood fill (visits, queue maximum), a recursive flood fill (max depth, RecursionError reported instead of crashing), run-length labeling, union-find over raw pixels, the naive single pass, and image builders (random disks, separated disks, a one-pixel-wide snake, U shapes, diagonal stripes). ORACLES: (1) partition equality (never label numbers) against the BFS on a 160 x 120 image of 60 disks (5,520 foreground pixels) under 4- and 8-connectivity, on 40 random 64 x 48 images under both (80 pairs), and on 10, 25, and 40 separated disks whose counts are known by construction: 88 comparisons, with run-length labeling and pixel union-find agreeing too; (2) counts: 28 / 27 components; two-pass 38,400 visits (exactly 2 per pixel, asserted) against BFS 41,280 / 63,360 (queue max 30 / 50); provisional labels 179 / 78, unions 151 / 51, finds 7,934 / 7,474 at 0.635 / 0.405 links per find (asserted under 1.5); unions == sets made minus components asserted for every method; run-length 499 runs, 471 / 472 unions, 1,443 / 1,455 finds; pixel union-find 5,520 sets, 5,492 / 5,493 unions, 25,588 / 45,026 finds at 0.824 / 0.889 links; recursive fill 41,280 / 63,360 visits (equal to BFS, asserted), depth 597 / 573; (3) snake 160 x 40 (3,220 pixels, one component): two-pass 12,800 visits, 11 labels, 10 unions; BFS queue max 1; recursive fill depth 3,220 at limit 50,000 and RecursionError at the default 1,000 (asserted); (4) diagonal stripes 60 x 60 period 3: 1,200 components under 4-connectivity (every pixel alone), 39 under 8 (asserted against the stripe count); (5) negative example: naive single pass 60 labels for 30 U shapes (asserted at least 2 per U) and 78 for 27 blobs under 8-connectivity; the two-pass made the same 60 provisional labels and 30 unions on the U image. Honest: author correction recorded (the draft expected about one provisional label per component; measured several per blob, 179 for 28 under 4-connectivity, because every row where a blob widens on its left starts a label). Cards: self, Flood fill, Union-find (live lesson badge, puzzle 8), Run-length encoding (all algoName; pages verified in dist/algo). neverUse: one raster pass with no equivalence table (60 labels for 30 U shapes), with the recursive flood fill crash as its cousin. Figure: pass one on a U shape with labels 1 and 2 and the amber union at the corner, beside a log-scale chart of sets made and finds spent (two-pass 78 / 7,474; run-length 499 / 1,455; pixel union-find 5,520 / 45,026); cite Rosenfeld and Pfaltz JACM 1966 DOI 10.1145/321356.321357, He, Chao, Suzuki IEEE TIP 2008, Wu, Otoo, Suzuki PAA 2009.
